# Hierarchical and Block-Based Data Structures

Also called: Hierarchical Grids

## Overview
Hierarchical and block-based data structures organize volumetric data into a multi-resolution hierarchy of uniform blocks (bricks) or spatial subdivisions (octrees) to accelerate ray traversal and rendering [G]. This approach is considered a good compromise preferred by many practitioners [S1, unofficial]. It enables efficient empty-space skipping, early ray termination, and adaptive resolution sampling by allowing the renderer to skip large empty regions or sample coarse data for distant objects [G]. It balances memory overhead and traversal complexity compared to unstructured meshes [KD-Tree Partitioned Volume Rendering](1966-kd-tree-partitioned-volume-rendering.md) and pure grid methods [Ray Grid Traversal with Adaptive Step Sizing](12497-ray-grid-traversal-with-adaptive-step-sizing.md) [G].

## Shared principles
All methods in this family share the following mechanisms:

1. **Spatial Subdivision:** The volume is partitioned into smaller, manageable units [G]. These units are either uniform blocks (bricks) of fixed size or spatial nodes in a tree structure (octree/quadtree) [G].
2. **Hierarchical Aggregation:** Parent nodes or blocks store aggregate metadata derived from their children [G]. Common metadata includes:
    * **Scalar Range:** Minimum and maximum values ($min, max$) of the scalar field within the subtree [G].
    * **Occupancy/Visibility:** Flags indicating if the block contains non-empty or non-transparent data [G].
3. **Traversal:** Ray traversal follows the hierarchy from root to leaf [G].
    * If a node is determined to be empty or irrelevant (e.g., threshold out of range, fully transparent), its children are skipped [G].
    * If a node is relevant, the ray is tested against its children [G].
4. **Adaptive Resolution:** Higher resolution data is stored in smaller, deeper nodes (leaves), while coarser data is stored in larger, shallower nodes [G]. This allows the renderer to select the appropriate resolution based on distance from the camera or visual importance [G].

## Subtopics

### [Ray-marching reference (min-max octree accelerated)](1554-ray-marching-reference-min-max-octree-accelerated.md)
[Ray-marching reference (min-max octree accelerated)](1554-ray-marching-reference-min-max-octree-accelerated.md) uses a min-max octree to accelerate direct isosurface visualization. It differs from siblings by guaranteeing continuous isosurfaces via binary search refinement within leaf nodes, avoiding the topological artifacts of mesh extraction. It is chosen when a baseline for general scalar volume isosurface rendering with low auxiliary memory overhead is required.

### [ExaBricks Rendering with RTX BVH](2577-exabricks-rendering-with-rtx-bvh.md)
[ExaBricks Rendering with RTX BVH](2577-exabricks-rendering-with-rtx-bvh.md) renders Adaptive Block-Refined (ABR) data using hardware-accelerated RTX BVH traversal. It distinguishes itself by replacing software-based tree traversal with dedicated RT Cores, avoiding complex control flow in shaders. It is chosen for interactive editing of transfer functions on large ABR datasets, provided the BVH can be rebuilt efficiently.

### [Brick Size and Octree Limit Tuning](4263-brick-size-and-octree-limit-tuning.md)
[Brick Size and Octree Limit Tuning](4263-brick-size-and-octree-limit-tuning.md) focuses on empirically selecting optimal brick dimensions and octree depth limits to mitigate hardware-specific bottlenecks like 3D texture sampling penalties. It differs from siblings by treating brick size and octree limit as orthogonal parameters to be tuned for specific GPU architectures. It is chosen when optimizing GPU-based volume rendering for specific hardware constraints.

### [Residency Octree](4950-residency-octree.md)
[Residency Octree](4950-residency-octree.md) is a hybrid structure for out-of-core DVR that decouples cache residency from spatial subdivision. Unlike standard octrees, each node represents a resolution-independent spatial region and references all resolution levels. It enables efficient mixing of channel resolutions and cache-miss compensation. It is chosen for multi-volume out-of-core rendering where flexible mixed-resolution access is critical.

### [Multiresolution with Octree Bricking](6106-multiresolution-with-octree-bricking.md)
[Multiresolution with Octree Bricking](6106-multiresolution-with-octree-bricking.md) encodes volumetric data at varying resolutions into a spatial octree, explicitly linking octree depth to resolution levels. It relies on software-managed out-of-core loading. It is chosen for large datasets exceeding texture memory where adaptive resolution based on viewer distance is needed.

### [Hierarchical Data Loading and Abstraction](19544-hierarchical-data-loading-and-abstraction.md)
[Hierarchical Data Loading and Abstraction](19544-hierarchical-data-loading-and-abstraction.md) provides a software architecture for abstracting Adaptive Mesh Refinement (AMR) simulation data into physical objects, separating dataset metadata from geometric structure. It solves the problem of efficient, on-demand access to hierarchical volumetric data by mediating all I/O through a lazy-loaded hierarchy. It is chosen for reproducible analysis of astrophysical simulation data without reinventing specialized scripts.

### [First Active Voxel Detection](4196-first-active-voxel-detection.md)
[First Active Voxel Detection](4196-first-active-voxel-detection.md) accelerates the initial hit detection in hierarchical structures by quickly identifying the first non-empty voxel along a ray. It differs from siblings by focusing on minimizing traversal overhead before full volume integration begins. It is chosen when ray initialization latency dominates rendering time.

### [Hierarchical DDA with Super-brick Skipping](5197-hierarchical-dda-with-super-brick-skipping.md)
[Hierarchical DDA with Super-brick Skipping](5197-hierarchical-dda-with-super-brick-skipping.md) extends discrete ray traversal by skipping entire super-bricks (clusters of bricks) when they are known to be empty. It sets itself apart by combining DDA efficiency with hierarchical pruning. It is chosen for structured hierarchical grids where large empty regions are common.

### [Octree-based traversal](5348-octree-based-traversal.md)
[Octree-based traversal](5348-octree-based-traversal.md) uses a standard octree structure for ray traversal, recursively visiting nodes only if the ray intersects their bounding boxes. It differs from siblings by relying on a pure tree structure without fixed brick boundaries. It is chosen for highly irregular or sparse volumetric data.

### [Empty Space Skipping via Data Structures](5619-empty-space-skipping-via-data-structures.md)
[Empty Space Skipping via Data Structures](5619-empty-space-skipping-via-data-structures.md) focuses on various acceleration structures specifically designed to maximize empty space skipping. It distinguishes itself by evaluating different data layouts (e.g., sparse grids, hash maps) for skip efficiency. It is chosen when memory bandwidth is limited and empty regions dominate the volume.

### [Multi-level Grid Structures](6354-multi-level-grid-structures.md)
[Multi-level Grid Structures](6354-multi-level-grid-structures.md) employs a hierarchy of uniform grids at different resolutions, similar to a mipmap chain but applied to spatial subdivision. It sets itself apart by maintaining strict uniformity at each level. It is chosen for regular datasets where hierarchical traversal overhead outweighs the benefits of irregular subdivision.

### [VIPER Ray-Traversal and Surface Intersection Algorithm](6590-viper-ray-traversal-and-surface-intersection-algorithm.md)
[VIPER Ray-Traversal and Surface Intersection Algorithm](6590-viper-ray-traversal-and-surface-intersection-algorithm.md) combines hierarchical traversal with precise surface intersection techniques. It differs from siblings by integrating ray marching and ray casting within the same hierarchical framework. It is chosen when high-fidelity surface rendering is required alongside volume integration.

### [Quadtree Raycasting](8208-quadtree-raycasting.md)
[Quadtree Raycasting](8208-quadtree-raycasting.md) applies quadtree subdivision to 2D slices or 3D projections for raycasting acceleration. It sets itself apart by using 2D spatial partitioning instead of 3D octrees. It is chosen for slice-based rendering or when memory constraints favor 2D structures.

### [Hierarchical Data Structure Traversal](11418-hierarchical-data-structure-traversal.md)
[Hierarchical Data Structure Traversal](11418-hierarchical-data-structure-traversal.md) provides a generalized framework for traversing various hierarchical acceleration structures. It differs from siblings by abstracting the traversal logic to support multiple data layouts. It is chosen when flexibility across different acceleration structures is required.

### Block-based GPU Volume Rendering with Acceleration
An efficient GPU rendering algorithm for large CT datasets that subdivides the volume into uniform blocks and accelerates rendering by combining early ray termination, empty-space skipping, and visibility culling to render only visible parts [S2, unofficial]. It achieves 3-4 frames per second on a 512 × 304 × 1878 dimension dataset using a Pentium 4 2.4 GHz PC with an NVIDIA Geforce 6600 [S2, unofficial].

### Block-based Alpha Histogram Construction
Uses spatial coherence to enhance histograms and transfer function design. The standard block size is $8^3$ voxels, but the minimum recommended size is $6^3$ to obtain good effect from spatial coherence; features of the same scale as the block size are favored [S3]. Anisotropic blocks (e.g., 3-4 times larger in the z-direction) can be used if tissue has a larger extent in a certain dimension [S3].

## Background
Hierarchical grids are considered a good compromise preferred by many practitioners for volume rendering acceleration [S1, unofficial]. The concept of hierarchical bounding volumes, where children are contained within parents, has roots in general ray tracing algorithms, including recursive inorder traversal methods by Kaplan, Arvo, and Jansen [S1, unofficial]. The specific application to volume rendering involves subdividing the volume into uniform blocks to take advantage of early ray termination and empty-space skipping, as demonstrated in efficient GPU rendering algorithms for large CT datasets [S2, unofficial]. The use of block-based structures for alpha-histograms to enhance transfer function design was further explored in the context of spatial coherence [S3].
